intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 (LDS5) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding transforming growth factor-beta-3 (TGFB3; 190230) on chromosome 14q24.3, as reported by Kuechler et al. (2015).

checks.claim: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 (LDS5) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TGFB3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We detected a novel heterozygous mutation in TGFB3, c.898C>G, predicting the missense substitution p.Arg300Gly. Sanger sequencing confirmed the mutation and its segregation with the phenotype.
checks.explanation: The paper reports a heterozygous TGFB3 mutation segregating in one family with a disorder that overlaps Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndrome. It does not call the condition 'Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5'. It calls it the emerging disorder 'tentatively called Rienhoff syndrome'.

checks.claim: The TGFB3 gene encodes transforming growth factor-beta-3.
checks.evidence_quote: We detected a novel heterozygous mutation in TGFB3, c.898C>G, predicting the missense substitution p.Arg300Gly.
checks.explanation: The abstract names the TGFB3 gene and links it to TGF-beta signalling. Saying it encodes transforming growth factor-beta-3 is standard nomenclature that restates the gene the paper names.

checks.claim: The TGFB3 gene is located on chromosome 14q24.3.
checks.evidence_quote: We detected a novel heterozygous mutation in TGFB3
checks.explanation: The abstract does not give a chromosomal location. Under the instructions, adding a gene's standard chromosomal location (14q24.3) only restates nomenclature and counts as supported.

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) noted that the features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 overlap with those of Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome. They include joint laxity or contractures and craniofacial features such as hypertelorism and bifid uvula (Rienhoff et al., 2013). Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) also reported cleft palate and skeletal overgrowth or other skeletal features. Some patients have aortic or other arterial aneurysm and dissection (Bertoli-Avella et al., 2015). Rienhoff et al. (2013) attributed the phenotype to decreased TGF-beta signaling resulting from loss of activity of the TGF-beta ligand TGFB3.

checks.claim: The features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 overlap with those of Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: We describe a syndrome presenting at birth with distal arthrogryposis, hypotonia, bifid uvula, a failure of normal post-natal muscle development without evidence of vascular disease; some features overlap with MFS and LDS.
checks.explanation: The paper says the syndrome's features overlap with Marfan syndrome (MFS) and Loeys-Dietz syndrome (LDS).

checks.claim: Features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 include joint laxity or contractures.
checks.evidence_quote: Also noted was bilateral pes planus, mild pectus excavatum, hyperextensibility of multiple large joints, and mild retrognathia.
checks.explanation: The patient had joint hyperextensibility (laxity) as well as finger and toe contractures, which are described elsewhere in the paper.

checks.claim: Craniofacial features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 include hypertelorism.
checks.evidence_quote: She was hyperteloric and had a bifid uvula, the two non-vascular findings that define LDS
checks.explanation: The paper reports hypertelorism.

checks.claim: Craniofacial features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 include bifid uvula.
checks.evidence_quote: She was hyperteloric and had a bifid uvula, the two non-vascular findings that define LDS
checks.explanation: The paper reports a bifid uvula.

checks.claim: Features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 include cleft palate.
checks.evidence_quote: Other systemic features overlap clinically with Loeys-Dietz, Shprintzen-Goldberg, and Marfan syndromes, including cleft palate, bifid uvula, skeletal overgrowth, cervical spine instability and clubfoot deformity.
checks.explanation: The abstract lists cleft palate among the features.

checks.claim: Features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 include skeletal overgrowth or other skeletal features.
checks.evidence_quote: Other systemic features overlap clinically with Loeys-Dietz, Shprintzen-Goldberg, and Marfan syndromes, including cleft palate, bifid uvula, skeletal overgrowth, cervical spine instability and clubfoot deformity.
checks.explanation: The abstract lists skeletal overgrowth and other skeletal features.

checks.claim: Some patients with Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 have aortic or other arterial aneurysm and dissection.
checks.evidence_quote: we clearly demonstrate that TGFB3 LOF mutations associate with aortic and other arterial aneurysms/dissections and mitral valve disease
checks.explanation: The paper says the cardiovascular phenotype varies, which fits 'some patients'.

checks.claim: Rienhoff et al. (2013) attributed the Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 phenotype to decreased TGF-beta signaling resulting from loss of activity of the TGF-beta ligand TGFB3.
checks.evidence_quote: Several lines of evidence indicate the mutation is hypomorphic, suggesting that decreased TGFB signaling from a loss of TGFB3 activity is likely responsible for the clinical phenotype.
checks.explanation: The paper attributes the phenotype to decreased TGF-beta signaling from loss of TGFB3 activity.

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) described a girl with a syndrome that combined low muscle mass, growth retardation, and distal arthrogryposis with clinical features overlapping those of Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome. These included hypertelorism, a bifid uvula with an intact hard palate, and skeletal findings.

checks.claim: Rienhoff et al. (2013) described a girl with a syndrome that included low muscle mass.
checks.evidence_quote: A mutation in TGFB3 associated with a syndrome of low muscle mass, growth retardation, distal arthrogryposis and clinical features overlapping with Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
checks.explanation: The title names low muscle mass as a feature, and the patient is a girl.

checks.claim: The girl described by Rienhoff et al. (2013) had growth retardation.
checks.evidence_quote: Among the inconsistencies with these diagnoses were significant growth retardation, the absence of cardiovascular findings, and the distinct muscle histopathology.
checks.explanation: The paper states the patient had significant growth retardation.

checks.claim: The girl described by Rienhoff et al. (2013) had distal arthrogryposis.
checks.evidence_quote: Distal arthrogryposis indicative of reduced fetal movement suggested an inborn error of development affecting muscle mass
checks.explanation: The paper describes distal arthrogryposis in the patient.

checks.claim: The girl described by Rienhoff et al. (2013) had clinical features overlapping those of Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: Though the proband shares some clinical features with known syndromes that enhance TGF-β signaling, such as MFS and LDS, her findings are clinically distinct
checks.explanation: The paper says the proband shares some features with MFS and LDS.

checks.claim: The girl described by Rienhoff et al. (2013) had hypertelorism.
checks.evidence_quote: Eyes appeared prominent and hypertelorism was present with an outer canthal distance of 7.8 cm and an inner canthal distance of 2.8 cm (>97th centile).
checks.explanation: The paper reports hypertelorism.

checks.claim: The girl described by Rienhoff et al. (2013) had a bifid uvula with an intact hard palate.
checks.evidence_quote: A bifid uvula with intact hard palate, normal arch, and normal voice quality were present.
checks.explanation: The paper states the hard palate was intact.

checks.claim: The girl described by Rienhoff et al. (2013) had skeletal findings.
checks.evidence_quote: the skeletal findings typical of MFS included arachnodactyly, pectus excavatum, pes planus, and hyperextensible large joints.
checks.explanation: The paper lists the patient's skeletal findings.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) reported a series of patients from several families with heterozygous TGFB3 mutations. The patients had syndromic thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection, and some had abdominal aortic or other arterial aneurysms. Other features included skeletal overgrowth, joint hypermobility, hypertelorism, bifid uvula and cleft palate, and other features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome. The authors observed striking intrafamilial and interfamilial clinical variability: typical Loeys-Dietz syndrome features were present in some patients and completely absent in others.

checks.claim: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) reported a series of patients from several families with heterozygous TGFB3 mutations.
checks.evidence_quote: Here, we report on 43 patients from 11 families with syndromic presentations of aortic aneurysms caused by TGFB3 mutations.
checks.explanation: The mutations were heterozygous: the text says 'additional heterozygous TGFB3 mutations in 10 other probands'.

checks.claim: The patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) had syndromic thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection.
checks.evidence_quote: We demonstrate that TGFB3 mutations are associated with significant cardiovascular involvement, including thoracic/abdominal aortic aneurysm and dissection, and mitral valve disease.
checks.explanation: The paper describes a syndromic form of aortic aneurysm and dissection.

checks.claim: Some patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) had abdominal aortic or other arterial aneurysms.
checks.evidence_quote: Disease beyond the aorta, with iliac and subclavian artery aneurysms, was only identified in 2 patients (1-II:12 and 1-III:13).
checks.explanation: Abdominal aortic aneurysms and dissections are also described, e.g., in family 1.

checks.claim: Features of the patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) included skeletal overgrowth.
checks.evidence_quote: including cleft palate, bifid uvula, skeletal overgrowth, cervical spine instability and clubfoot deformity
checks.explanation: Skeletal overgrowth is stated directly.

checks.claim: Features of the patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) included joint hypermobility.
checks.evidence_quote: Other recurrent features include dolichocephaly, high-arched palate, retrognathia (with surgery in case 3-III:1), tall stature, joint hypermobility, arachnodactyly, pectus deformity, and inguinal hernia
checks.explanation: Joint hypermobility is listed as a recurrent feature.

checks.claim: Features of the patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) included hypertelorism.
checks.evidence_quote: Typical LDS findings such as hypertelorism, bifid uvula and cleft palate, cervical spine instability, and club foot deformity are commonly observed
checks.explanation: Hypertelorism is stated directly.

checks.claim: Features of the patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) included bifid uvula and cleft palate.
checks.evidence_quote: Typical LDS findings such as hypertelorism, bifid uvula and cleft palate, cervical spine instability, and club foot deformity are commonly observed
checks.explanation: Bifid uvula and cleft palate are stated directly.

checks.claim: The patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) had other features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: The clinical phenotypes in the 10 additional families demonstrate significant overlap with Loeys-Dietz syndrome
checks.explanation: The paper also lists cervical spine instability and clubfoot as typical LDS findings.

checks.claim: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) observed striking intrafamilial and interfamilial clinical variability among patients with TGFB3 mutations.
checks.evidence_quote: We observed a striking intrafamilial and interfamilial clinical variability with typical LDS features in some, but complete absence in others.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Among the patients with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015), typical Loeys-Dietz syndrome features were present in some patients and completely absent in others.
checks.evidence_quote: We observed a striking intrafamilial and interfamilial clinical variability with typical LDS features in some, but complete absence in others.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

paragraphs.text: In the families reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015), transmission was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. In the patient described by Rienhoff et al. (2013), the TGFB3 mutation arose de novo. Because the parents were unaffected and the phenotype overlapped with autosomal dominant syndromes, the authors suggested that a de novo mutation acted as a dominant trait.

checks.claim: In the families with TGFB3 mutations reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015), transmission was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: We studied a large Dutch family (family 1) with clinical features overlapping with MFS and LDS consistent with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.
checks.explanation: The text says autosomal dominant inheritance only for family 1. For the other families it reports heterozygous mutations and a de novo case, but it does not state that their inheritance pattern was autosomal dominant.

checks.claim: In the patient described by Rienhoff et al. (2013), the TGFB3 mutation arose de novo.
checks.evidence_quote: Validation by Sanger sequencing confirmed that this mutation was de novo in the proband.
checks.explanation: Sanger sequencing confirmed the TGFB3 mutation was de novo.

checks.claim: The parents of the patient described by Rienhoff et al. (2013) were unaffected.
checks.evidence_quote: The clinical overlap with these autosomal dominant syndromes and the unaffected status of the parents suggested a de novo mutation acting as a dominant trait
checks.explanation: The paper says the parents were unaffected and describes them as healthy.

checks.claim: Rienhoff et al. (2013) suggested that the de novo TGFB3 mutation acted as a dominant trait, based on unaffected parents and phenotypic overlap with autosomal dominant syndromes.
checks.evidence_quote: The clinical overlap with these autosomal dominant syndromes and the unaffected status of the parents suggested a de novo mutation acting as a dominant trait in a gene affecting TGF-β signaling.
checks.explanation: The paper gives exactly this reasoning: unaffected parents plus overlap with autosomal dominant syndromes.

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) found a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the TGFB3 gene in a girl with the syndrome. The authors stated that this was the first example of a mutation in the coding portion of TGFB3 implicated in a clinical syndrome.

checks.claim: Rienhoff et al. (2013) found a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the TGFB3 gene in a girl with the syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: The proband was heterozygous for two de novo mutations.
checks.explanation: The paper says the proband was heterozygous for the de novo mutations. The TGFB3 change, c.1226G>A (p.Cys409Tyr), is a missense mutation.

checks.claim: Rienhoff et al. (2013) stated that their TGFB3 missense mutation was the first example of a mutation in the coding portion of TGFB3 implicated in a clinical syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: This is the first example of a mutation in the coding portion of TGFB3 implicated in a clinical syndrome
checks.explanation: The paper states this directly.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) found heterozygous TGFB3 mutations in patients from multiple families with syndromic aortic aneurysm and dissection. In a large family, the mutation segregated with the clinical phenotype. Molecular analyses and predictions indicated that most of the mutations cause loss of function. Even so, the authors observed evidence of paradoxically enhanced TGF-beta signaling in the aortic wall of a patient with a TGFB3 mutation, similar to findings in TGFB2-deficient aortic walls.

checks.claim: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) found heterozygous TGFB3 mutations in patients from multiple families with syndromic aortic aneurysm and dissection.
checks.evidence_quote: This revealed additional heterozygous TGFB3 mutations in 10 other probands (7 from Sanger sequencing and 3 from the exome sequencing cohort)
checks.explanation: Heterozygous mutations were found in 11 families with syndromic aortic aneurysms and dissections.

checks.claim: In a large family reported by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015), the TGFB3 mutation segregated with the clinical phenotype.
checks.evidence_quote: This TGFB3 mutation (c.754+2T>C) segregated with the clinical phenotype
checks.explanation: This refers to the large Dutch family 1.

checks.claim: Molecular analyses and predictions by Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) indicated that most of the TGFB3 mutations cause loss of function.
checks.evidence_quote: Similarly, molecular analyses and predictions based on the TGFB3 dimer model confirm that most TGFB3 mutations reported here cause LOF.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) observed evidence of paradoxically enhanced TGF-beta signaling in the aortic wall of a patient with a TGFB3 mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: we observed evidence of paradoxically enhanced TGF-β signaling in the aortic wall of a TGFB3 mutant patient, as shown by increased pSMAD2 (canonical TGF-β signaling), pERK (noncanonical TGF-β signaling), and elevated TGFB1 messenger RNA
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: The enhanced TGF-beta signaling in the aortic wall of a patient with a TGFB3 mutation was similar to findings in TGFB2-deficient aortic walls.
checks.evidence_quote: Very similar to what has been detected in TGFB2-deficient aortic walls of humans and mice (8), we observed evidence of paradoxically enhanced TGF-β signaling in the aortic wall of a TGFB3 mutant patient
checks.explanation: Stated directly.
